categorias.descripcion: Learn to work with AI by doing: from a chat window to code you own, one first step at a time.

workspace.linea: Work in a folder your AI remembers

connect.linea: Make tools talk to each other

publish.linea: Put your work where others can use it

piezas.descripcion: The first long video of the series: prompts you paste, and the AI does the work.
piezas.texto: If you use ChatGPT or Claude in a chat window every day, you know the feeling: each new chat starts from zero, and you explain your project again. This first long video shows another way to work. You paste a few prompts, and your AI sets up a private folder, writes a memory file it reads every time, and does a first real task while you watch and approve each step. You will not type a single command. You will learn what to expect at each stage, how long it takes, what can go wrong, and how to undo it. Claude Code is the worked example; the ideas carry over to other tools.

hojas: An AI that can work in a folder
One prompt sets up the workspace
A notebook the AI reads every session
You decide what goes in it
Ask it to show its work
Nothing installed, deleted or sent without asking

piezas.descripcion: Save a first version of your work in a private repository.
piezas.texto: A commit is a saved snapshot of your work, with a short note saying what changed. Once you have one, you can always go back. In this piece you ask your AI to make the first commit in a private repository, read the note it proposes, and check what was saved before you agree. You will see the difference between a file that changed and a change that was saved, and why small commits with clear messages make mistakes cheap to fix. There are no commands to memorize: the AI runs them and explains each one in plain words.

hojas: A note that says what changed
A history you can return to
Leave out secrets and large files
It shows the change and waits for your OK
You choose who can see it

fuentes.titulo: Pro Git, 2.2 Recording Changes to the Repository

piezas.descripcion: Set up a place where Claude can read and change your files safely.
piezas.texto: Before your AI can help with real files, it needs a place to work: one folder, with clear limits on what it may do. This piece walks through setting up that place, with Claude Code as the example. You will see how to sign in, how to open a project folder, how to choose which actions it may take without asking you, and how a short memory file keeps your preferences between sessions. The focus is safety: start in a practice folder, keep keys out of the chat, and read every change before you accept it. By the end you have a workspace you understand and trust.

hojas: A project file it reads each time
No keys or passwords in chat

piezas.descripcion: Put a simple web page online for free.
piezas.texto: A web page can be one small file. GitHub Pages puts it online for free from a public repository, at an address you can share. In this piece your AI writes a simple page with you, saves it in a repository and turns on Pages, while you check each step. You will learn just enough HTML to read what it wrote, where the page lives, how long it takes to appear, and what to do when it does not. We also cover what should never go on a public page: personal details, keys and private notes, because everything in a public repository can be seen.

hojas: Turn it on in the repository
Ask the AI to read the error

piezas.descripcion: What a token is, why it matters, and how to keep it secret.
piezas.texto: An access token is a long secret string that lets a program act on your behalf, the way a key opens a door. Websites and AI tools ask for one when your code needs to read data or publish something. This piece shows what a token is, how to create one with the fewest permissions that will do the job, where to keep it so it never lands in a chat or a public file, and what to do if it leaks: revoke it at once and create a new one with an expiration date. Small habits, and they protect everything else you build.

hojas: A secret that acts for you
In a secrets store or settings page

piezas.descripcion: How one program asks another for data, in plain words.
piezas.texto: An API is a way for one program to ask another for something and get an answer back in a format both understand. When a weather app shows tomorrow's rain, it asked a weather service through an API. This piece explains the idea in plain words: a request goes to an address, and the answer comes back, often as JSON, a simple text format of names and values. You will learn the few words you keep seeing (endpoint, request, response, status code, key) and why some APIs are open to anyone while others need a token.

fuentes.titulo: RFC 8259: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format

piezas.descripcion: Call a few free public APIs and see what comes back.
piezas.texto: The fastest way to understand APIs is to call a few. In this piece your AI makes requests to free public APIs that need no account for personal use, such as a weather forecast and open data from the U.S. Treasury, and shows you the raw answer next to a readable version. You will learn to read what came back, spot an error, respect the limits each service sets, and give credit where the terms ask for it. Then you ask your AI to turn one answer into a small table or chart you can keep, with its source and date.

hojas: Read the docs and terms first

piezas.titulo: From one email to a campaign
piezas.descripcion: From asking an AI to help with one email you paste and send, to planning a segmented campaign of thousands of personalized emails, sent in batches with a person approving each one.
piezas.texto: Most people start by asking an AI to polish one email, which they paste and send. This piece follows the path from there to a full campaign: turning a messy list of contacts into clean segments, writing a message for each segment, personalizing thousands of HTML emails, and sending them in small batches. A person stays in the loop at every step, reviewing samples and approving each batch before it leaves. We cover consent, unsubscribe links and anti-spam law such as CAN-SPAM in the US and the GDPR in the EU, because a message only helps when the person agreed to hear from you.

mapa.raiz: From one email to a campaign

hojas: Ask the AI for a draft

fuentes.titulo: CAN-SPAM Act: A Compliance Guide for Business
Information for individuals: your rights under the GDPR

categorias.descripcion: The basics of reading a market, explained plainly. Education only, never advice.

piezas.descripcion: Where a market price comes from and what it tells you.
piezas.texto: The price you see on a screen is usually the last trade: the most recent moment a buyer and a seller agreed. Behind it sit two other numbers, the highest price someone is bidding and the lowest price someone is asking, and the gap between them. This piece explains where a market price comes from, why the price you get can differ from the one you saw, and how some prices are set another way, like the daily reference rates a central bank publishes. Education only: nothing here tells you what to buy or sell.

hojas: A buyer and a seller agreed
Market order: fast, price not fixed
Limit order: price fixed, fill not sure

piezas.descripcion: Lines, time frames and scales, and what each one hides.
piezas.texto: A chart is a drawing of prices over time, and every drawing makes choices. A line chart shows closes and hides what happened in between. A one-minute view and a one-week view tell different stories about the same market. On a linear scale a steady percentage rise looks like it is speeding up; a log scale shows equal percentage moves as equal steps. And an axis that does not start at zero can make a small move look large. This piece teaches you to ask what a chart leaves out before you trust it. Education only, never advice.

hojas: How a small move can look big

piezas.descripcion: Open, high, low and close in one shape.
piezas.texto: A candle packs four prices into one shape: where a period opened, its high, its low, and where it closed. The body runs from open to close; the thin lines above and below, called wicks, reach the high and the low. In this piece you learn to read one candle, then a row of them, and to see what a candle cannot show, such as whether the high or the low came first. We also look at what researchers found when popular candle patterns were tested on large US stocks: on their own, they were not generally profitable. Education only, never advice.

hojas: The time frame sets each candle
Which came first, high or low

piezas.descripcion: How common strategies work. No strategy is perfect; try any of them on a demo or paper account first.
piezas.texto: A trading strategy is a set of rules: when to enter, when to exit, and how much to risk. This piece describes how a few common kinds work, such as following a trend, expecting a return to the average, and trading a breakout, and where each one tends to fail. Then it looks at the evidence: individual investors who traded the most earned less, most people who kept day trading lost money, and a backtest can look perfect while saying little about the future. Hence the rule here, paper first: test any idea on a demo or paper account before real money. Education only, never advice.

hojas: Most persistent day traders lost money

piezas.descripcion: An open indicator that labels the market's state, with its code in Python and Pine v6.
piezas.texto: Many indicators assume the market is trending, and they struggle when it moves sideways. This open indicator asks an earlier question: what state is the market in right now? It labels each period as trending, ranging or unclear, like a traffic light, using two plain measures: how efficiently price has moved, and how wide its recent swings are compared with their own history. You get the code in Python and in Pine Script v6, the rules in words, colors that work for colorblind readers, and the cases where it gets things wrong. It describes the market and gives no buy or sell signals.

fuentes.titulo: Pine Script v6 User Manual: First steps
Color Universal Design: how to make figures and presentations that are friendly to colorblind people

categorias.descripcion: Behaviors and habits, each with the studies behind it.

piezas.descripcion: Each behavior with the peer-reviewed studies behind it. Drafted by NAOS, read and signed by N.
piezas.texto: NAOS Shorts carry small behaviors: a slower breath, naming a feeling, giving worry its own time. Each article takes one behavior and lays out the study behind it: who took part, what they did, what was measured, what changed, and what the study cannot tell us. NAOS drafts each article, and N reads and signs it. The aim is that you can judge the evidence yourself, try the behavior with realistic expectations, and know when a practice is not enough and it is time to talk to a professional.

fuentes.autor: Melis Yilmaz Balban et al., Cell Reports Medicine

fuentes.titulo: Stimulus control applications to the treatment of worry
fuentes.autor: T. D. Borkovec et al., Behaviour Research and Therapy

piezas.descripcion: Longer sessions built from the behavior Shorts, to follow along.
piezas.texto: Some behaviors work better with time than in a 60-second Short. These long sessions join several of them into one guided practice you can follow from start to finish: slow breathing with longer exhales, resting attention on the breath and coming back when the mind wanders, naming what you feel, and letting someone steady you. Each step names the study it comes from and keeps its claim modest. You can pause at any point, and the steps are written out to download. These are practices for calm and do not replace therapy; if anxiety is heavy, talk to a professional.

hojas: One word for what you feel
A hand, a walk, a call

piezas.descripcion: Looped affirmations rooted in peer-reviewed findings. A gentle review before sleep. The promise is review only; we do not claim you learn while asleep.
piezas.texto: This piece is a quiet loop of short affirmations for the end of the day, drawn from findings you have met in NAOS videos. It is meant as a gentle review before sleep. We are careful about the promise: research shows sleep helps keep what you learned while awake, and in one study people did not consciously remember words they heard while falling asleep, so the value lies in the review you do while still awake. You will also find short notes on self-affirmation, and on a five-minute bedtime writing habit that helped people fall asleep faster.
